- Conditional statements are good for many purposes in coding:
  - conditional iteration
  - binning data
  - catching errors

:::notes
Conditionally iterating over data can be a powerful tool, for such things as
catching errors, testing a user input, or, perhaps more commonly in data
analysis tasks, creating categorical values from numeric interval or ratio data.
:::

```{r, echo = FALSE}
# load the data
gap_dat <- read.csv(file = "../../data/gapminder.csv")
```

## `if ... else` construct

```{r}
if("Afghanistan" %in% gap_dat$country){
  print("Afghanistan in dataset")
}else{
  print("Afghanistan not in dataset")
}
```

:::notes
`if else` statements apply a test to a value, and if it returns `TRUE`,
one thing is done, and if it returns `FALSE` an alternative thing is done. 
Although this syntax is useful it is limited in it's applications.
:::

## *problem*: `if` needs exactly one `TRUE` or `FALSE`

```{r, error = TRUE}
# a whole column is many values, so if() doesn't know which to use
if (gap_dat$lifeExp > 60) "long" else "short"

# NA is neither TRUE nor FALSE
x <- NA
if (x > 5) print("big")
```

:::notes
The problem is that `if ... else` asks a single yes/no question. Given a
whole column data it will fail, because it can't tell which of the answers you
meant (note that this ties in neatly to our discussion last week about
vectorization). A missing value fails too, because "is NA bigger than 5?" has no
answer. This is the line between this slide and the rest of the session:
`if` is for one value (an argument, a setting, a check), and `ifelse()`,
`case_when()` and `cut()` are for whole columns, the same vectorized idea from
the iteration session. Related: use `&&` and `||` to combine single values
inside `if`, and `&` and `|` to combine whole vectors.
:::

## A possible solution: chaining multiple `if` statements

```{r}
x <- 7

if (x < 6) {
  print("x is less than 6")
}
if (x == 5) {
  print("x is equal to 5")
}else{
  print("x is greater than not less than 6 and is not equal to 5")
}
```

:::notes
Although I don't recommend doing this, you can also chain multiple
(an infinite!) `if` statements together.
:::

## Iterating over vectors

```{r}
# create an empty variable to hold our ordered categorical data
gap_dat$income_level <- ordered(NA, levels = c("low-income",
                                                      "middle-income",
                                                      "high-income"))
# start the for loop to add values to income-level based on GDP values
for (i in seq_along(gap_dat$income_level)) { # for each item along the dataframe
  if (gap_dat$gdpPercap[i] <= 10000) { # if gdpPercap is LT = to 10000
    gap_dat$income_level[i] <- 'low-income' # add 'low-income' to that observation's income level variable
  }else if (gap_dat$gdpPercap[i] <= 75000) { # else, if gdpPercap is LT = 75000
    gap_dat$income_level[i] <- "middle-income" #  add 'middle-income' to that observation's income level variable
  }else { # otherwise
    gap_dat$income_level[i] <- "high-income"  #  add 'high-income' to that observation's income level variable
  }
}
summary(gap_dat$income_level)
```


:::notes
A more practical implementation of an if else statement would be creating a
new variable with values based off of those in another variable. This process
can get a little convoluted as it combines an `if else` statement with a
`for loop`.

As an example, lets assume that we want to categorize countries based on their
GDP as either high, middle, or low income. This can be cumbersome. Luckily R
offers some simpler options for iterating over data with an if else construct.
:::

## `ifelse()`

```{r}
# Assign values
# of 'below-average' if lifeExp is equal to or below 59.47 
# and 'above-average' if above 59.47
gap_dat$lifeExp_cat <- ifelse(gap_dat$lifeExp <= 59.47,
                              "below-average",
                              "above-average")

# assign appropriate data type
gap_dat$lifeExp_cat <- ordered(gap_dat$lifeExp_cat,
                               levels = c("below-average", "above-average"))

summary(gap_dat$lifeExp_cat)
```

:::notes
R has a built in function, `ifelse()` that allows us to provide a condition,
and, if that condition returns `TRUE` to do one thing, and if it returns `FALSE`
to do something else. We'll split life expectancy into 'above average' and
below average' categories.
:::

## `ifelse()` construct

```{r, warning=TRUE}
# create a numeric vector
some_numbers <- c(6:-4)

# take the square root of each value, which creates a bit of an issue
sqrt(some_numbers)
```

:::notes
`ifelse()` works well when we have a two condition set to work through. One more
example, pulled from its documentation, to help avoid an error / warning being
thrown or unwanted values being produced...
:::

# Solution: use `if_else()`

```{r}
# using if else to test for numbers greater than or equal to 0
# if true, calculate the square root
# if false, produce NA
sqrt(ifelse(some_numbers >= 0, some_numbers, NA))
```

:::notes
We can use `if_else()` to sort through data. Here we bin the data by those that
are above or below zero to avoid taking the `sqrt` of a negative number.
:::

# Same result, less code: `case_when()` and `cut()`

```{r}
income_cw <- dplyr::case_when(
  gap_dat$gdpPercap <= 10000 ~ "low-income",
  gap_dat$gdpPercap <= 75000 ~ "middle-income",
  .default = "high-income"
)

income_cw <- ordered(income_cw,
                     levels = c("low-income", "middle-income", "high-income"))

# cut() takes in a numeric value (gdpperCap)
# sets the bins (breaks)
# and assigns new levels
income_cut <- cut(gap_dat$gdpPercap,
                  breaks = c(-Inf, 10000, 75000, Inf),
                  labels = c("low-income", "middle-income", "high-income"),
                  ordered_result = TRUE)


identical(income_cw, gap_dat$income_level)  # same as the for loop?
identical(income_cut, gap_dat$income_level)
summary(income_cut)
```

:::notes
This is the income loop from earlier rewritten two ways. `case_when()` reads
top to bottom and stops at the first condition that's TRUE, so the order of
the lines matters, just like `else if`. `.default` catches everything left
over. `cut()` is base R's tool for binning numbers into ordered categories in
one call: `breaks` are the cut points, and by default each bin includes its
upper edge, which matches `<=` in the loop. `identical()` checks that all
three approaches agree, which is a good habit whenever you refactor code.
:::

# `case_when()`

```{r}
gap_dat$pop_size <- dplyr::case_when(
  gap_dat$pop <= 1000000 ~ "small",
  gap_dat$pop <= 100000000 ~ "medium",
  gap_dat$pop > 100000000 ~ "large"
)

gap_dat$pop_size <- ordered(gap_dat$pop_size, levels = c("small", "medium", "large"))

summary(gap_dat$pop_size)
```


:::notes
`case_when()` is a more compact version of using multiple if_else statements
that is native to `dplyr`.
:::

# `switch()`: choosing by name

```{r, error = TRUE}
# switch assigns values based on character string
summarise_col <- function(x, stat = "mean") {
  switch(stat,
         mean   = mean(x),     # if stat = 'mean'
         median = median(x),   # if stat = 'median'
         sd     = sd(x),
         # stop defines an error message if input is not accepted
         # can be captured by a log file
         stop("stat must be mean, median or sd, not ", stat))
}

summarise_col(gap_dat$lifeExp, "median")
summarise_col(gap_dat$lifeExp, "mod")
```

:::notes
When you're choosing between several options by name, `switch()` is cleaner
than a chain of `if (stat == "mean") ... else if (stat == "median") ...`.
R matches the first argument against the names and runs that one. An unnamed
last argument is the fallback, used here to give a helpful error. Like `if`,
`switch()` takes one value, not a vector, so it belongs inside functions, not
on columns. You can also leave an option empty, as in `Americas = , Europe =
"west"`, to have several names share one result.
:::

# Catching problems: `stop()`, `stopifnot()` and `warning()`

```{r, error = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
safe_log <- function(x) {
  # idicates output is not numeric
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x))                    # stop: can't continue
  if (any(x <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {            # warn: can continue
    # return descriptive custom warning
    warning("x has values <= 0; log() returns NaN or -Inf for those") 
  }
  # if x is numeric and > 0 return the log of x
  log(x)
}

safe_log(c(1, 10, 100))
safe_log("10")
safe_log(c(-1, 10))
```

:::notes
Conditions are how your own functions protect their users, including you.
`stop()` halts with a message when continuing would be meaningless;
`stopifnot()` is a shortcut for checks that should always be true. `warning()`
flags something suspicious but lets the code finish. Checking inputs at the
top of a function means errors show up where the mistake is made, with a
clear message, not three steps later as a confusing result. To handle an
error instead of stopping, look up `tryCatch()`.
:::

# Takeaway

- `if` / `else if` / `else` choose what to do for **one** value
  - the condition must be a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`: no vectors, no `NA`
  - use `&&` / `||` inside `if`, `&` / `|` for whole vectors
- For whole columns, use vectorized conditions:
  - `ifelse()` / `if_else()` for two outcomes
  - `case_when()` for many outcomes; order matters, first `TRUE` wins
  - `cut()` to bin numbers into ordered categories
- `switch()` chooses between options by name
- `stop()`, `stopifnot()` and `warning()` catch problems early with clear
messages
- When you rewrite code, check that the old and new versions agree with
`identical()`

:::notes
The main thing to remember from today is the split between single values and
whole vectors. `if` and `switch()` make one decision, which is why they live
inside functions: checking an argument, picking a method, stopping on bad
input. When you want a decision for every row of your data, reach for
`ifelse()`, `case_when()` or `cut()` instead of wrapping `if` in a for loop.
They're shorter, faster, and harder to get wrong.
:::
